lesson.title: The Brain's Main Accelerator: Glutamate and Excitatory Signaling
lesson.summary: Glutamate is the primary excitatory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system, responsible for the majority of the brain's fast signaling and for the synaptic changes that underlie learning and memory.
lesson.body:
Neurotransmitters can be broadly excitatory, pushing a receiving neuron's membrane potential toward threshold, or inhibitory, pushing it away. Glutamate is overwhelmingly the nervous system's main excitatory neurotransmitter, used at a very large share of the synapses throughout the brain and spinal cord, more than any other single neurotransmitter covered in this unit, which is part of why problems with glutamate signaling can have such widespread effects on brain function.

Glutamate follows the same general transmission cycle described earlier, but it acts on several distinct receptor types with different effects. AMPA receptors open quickly to let Na+ flow into the postsynaptic cell, producing a fast, standard excitatory postsynaptic potential, the same kind of EPSP discussed in the sections on depolarization and synaptic threshold. NMDA receptors behave differently: at normal resting potential a magnesium ion physically blocks their channel, and they only open fully once the postsynaptic membrane is already somewhat depolarized, at which point they allow both Na+ and calcium, Ca2+, to enter the cell.

That calcium influx through NMDA receptors plays a central role in long-term potentiation, a lasting strengthening of the connection between two neurons that occurs when they are repeatedly activated together. Long-term potentiation is widely considered a cellular basis for how learning and memory get stored in the brain, following the simplified principle that synapses which fire together strengthen together, with glutamate's NMDA receptor acting as part of the machinery that detects that coincidence and helps convert a brief pattern of activity into a more lasting change in the synapse.

Glutamate's excitatory power comes with a genuine risk. In excessive amounts, typically following an injury such as a stroke or a period of oxygen deprivation, overstimulation of glutamate receptors can allow dangerous amounts of calcium to build up inside neurons, damaging or killing them, a process known as excitotoxicity. This is one reason the nervous system tightly regulates glutamate levels and depends on efficient reuptake by transporter proteins, often located on nearby support cells as well as the presynaptic terminal, to clear it from the synapse quickly after each use.

This connects directly back to earlier material: the excitatory postsynaptic potentials described when covering synaptic threshold and summation are, at a typical excitatory synapse, very often produced by glutamate binding AMPA receptors. That means nearly every earlier example of small depolarizations adding up toward threshold across a neuron's dendrites was, in practice, glutamate doing exactly this job. It sits at the excitatory end of a balance with inhibitory neurotransmitters, and that balance shapes everything from momentary reflexes to lasting memories.
